doc.title: Paul Shaffer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 24, 2023

title: Piano conducting and the pace of the Letterman show
summary: Shaffer discusses conducting from the piano, ending cues with the drummer, and the rushed taping schedule.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Well even though you are piano conducting off Broadway style, piano conductors exist in the off Broadway scene. They don’t have the — again the union. On Broadway you’ve got to have a conductor, who gets double scale or whatever, but off Broadway because budgets are more limited, and that’s, you know even before “The Magic Show” I did one off Broadway show for Joe Papp in 1973. And you’re piano conducting. So if you’ve got one hand free you can conduct with the other hand but sometimes it’s got to be head, and certainly yes. And also you know in this case I’m watching them too. We haven’t run it with them after all, we ran it once with the band, so I don’t know when are they going to want it to stop. I’m just making sure, you know, “yes” bang. You know and then you have that going too. It’s tremendously exciting when I look back on it, it really was.
I guess. And when it finally got to the end you looked at the drummer, I guess it was Anton —
He gave some of that, yeah. Well they really had not been rehearsed.

When we rehearsed it I certainly didn’t rehearse an ending. I don’t know what will happen, you know, just watch me. And then the audience is in and that was another thing about Dave, when it was 5:00 or something and the show tape’s going to roll right at 5:30, the audience load in starts at 5. If I’m not finished with my, “Paul clear the stage, we’ve got to go.” I said, “I just need another.” “Get off!” That’s the way it was so it also made it tremendously exciting. Sometimes we didn’t have time even to learn the ending or something of a song and would go on in that position too. Crazy. Crazy. You get used to it on a daily basis.
